title: Almond rochers
subtitle: chocolate praline crunch balls
excerpt: Almond rochers are small mounds of chopped toasted almonds bound in caramelised praline, dipped in dark chocolate and rolled in more flaked almonds. They have a crisp, shattery outer shell and a chewy-crunchy interior. They keep well for two weeks, make 30 in one batch, and look considerably more impressive than the effort involved.
sourceNotes: Rochers (French for 'rocks') are a classic French confiserie, typically consisting of a nut-and-chocolate mixture shaped into irregular rounds resembling stones. They appear in French chocolate shop collections (particularly at Christmas and Easter) and are a standard entry-level project in French confectionery training. The praline base, sugar caramelised with almonds then ground to a paste, is the same technique behind the filling in many Belgian chocolates and French gateaux. The home version dips in melted chocolate rather than tempered couverture, which produces a slightly less glossy but equally delicious result.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in a single layer then transfer to a container. Defrost at room temperature for 1 hour.
recipe.batchNotes: Keep in an airtight container in a cool place for up to 2 weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 weeks ahead; they improve after the first day as the praline softens slightly.

content.text: Almond rochers are small chocolate-and-nut clusters with a praline centre and crunchy almond coating. The praline base is quick, caramelised sugar poured over toasted almonds and ground to a rough paste, and the dipping takes more care than skill. These last two weeks and are good gifts.

Preheat the oven to 160°C. Spread the blanched whole almonds on a baking tray and roast for 12 to 15 minutes until golden and fragrant. Set aside 100 g for the praline and roughly chop the rest to add to the chocolate mixture later.

Heat the sugar in a dry medium saucepan over a medium heat. Do not stir. Swirl the pan gently once the edges begin to melt. Cook to a deep amber, the colour of dark toffee. Add the 100 g of toasted whole almonds and a pinch of salt, stir once with an oiled spoon, then pour immediately onto a sheet of lightly oiled parchment. Spread out with a spatula and leave to cool completely. Break into pieces and process in a food processor to a coarse, sandy praline paste, some larger almond fragments are fine.

Melt 100 g of the dark chocolate in a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water. Stir in the praline paste and the reserved chopped toasted almonds. Mix until combined. The mixture should be stiff enough to scoop, if it's very loose, refrigerate for 15 minutes. Roll into balls, about 15 g each, place on parchment, and refrigerate for 30 minutes until firm.
Dip in chocolate and coat in flaked almonds

Melt the remaining 200 g dark chocolate. Put the toasted flaked almonds in a shallow bowl. Dip each praline ball in the melted chocolate, letting the excess drip off, then roll briefly in the flaked almonds. Place on parchment and leave to set at room temperature for 1 hour, or refrigerate for 20 minutes. They are ready when the chocolate coating is completely firm.
